nameStory: The word 'avocado' comes from the Aztec word 'ahuacatl,' which Spanish explorers adapted into 'aguacate' before it evolved into our modern English name. It's also called 'alligator pear' because of its bumpy, dark green skin that resembles an alligator's hide and its pear-like shape. This tropical fruit tree earned its place in the laurel family alongside spice plants like cinnamon and bay laurel.
description: The avocado is an evergreen tree in the laurel family, originally from Central and South America but occasionally grown as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in New England. In its native habitat, it can grow quite large, but indoor plants stay much smaller with glossy, oval leaves. The tree produces small, inconspicuous flowers and eventually the familiar green to black fruits we know from the grocery store - though indoor plants rarely fruit without special care.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery evergreen leaves that are oval-shaped with a glossy, dark green surface and paler underside. When crushed, they may release a faint spicy-sweet aroma typical of the laurel family.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: In New England, typically seen as a small potted tree or large houseplant with a single trunk and spreading branches. Indoor specimens rarely exceed a few feet tall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are green to brown and smooth, becoming slightly rougher with age. The bark feels firm but not deeply furrowed like outdoor trees.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Large, pear-shaped to oval fruits with bumpy or smooth skin ranging from green to dark purple-black. The flesh inside is creamy, buttery yellow-green when ripe.

habitat: In New England, avocado trees are found exclusively indoors as houseplants, in greenhouses, or conservatories where they can be protected from freezing temperatures. They require warm, humid conditions and bright indirect light. You might spot them in botanical gardens, plant shops, or enthusiastic gardeners' homes where they're grown from grocery store pits.

seasonality.spring: Indoor avocado plants may show new growth with fresh, bright green leaves emerging. Any flowering would occur during warmer months if conditions are right.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season for indoor plants, with the most vigorous leaf growth and best chance of flowering in greenhouse conditions.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows as daylight hours decrease. Plants may need to be moved closer to windows or supplemented with grow lights.
seasonality.winter: Growth nearly stops in the shorter days. Plants should be kept away from cold windows and heating vents to prevent stress.

funFact: Avocados are actually giant berries botanically speaking, and they evolved to be eaten by massive ice age mammals like giant ground sloths - the animals that could swallow the huge seed whole and spread it around were mostly extinct by the time humans arrived!
confusionNotes: Indoor avocado plants might be confused with other glossy-leaved houseplants like rubber trees or magnolia seedlings, but avocado leaves have that distinctive oval shape and the characteristic laurel family scent when crushed. Remember: if it smells faintly spicy-sweet when you rub a leaf, think laurel family.
contextualKnowledge: Most avocado 'trees' people grow in New England are started from the pit of a grocery store avocado using the popular toothpick-and-water method. However, these trees are unlikely to ever produce fruit indoors and are grown purely as novelty houseplants. The avocados we eat come from grafted trees grown in warm climates like California and Mexico.
compareHints: Avocado is the only member of the Persea genus you'll encounter in New England. Compared to other laurel family members like spicebush (which grows wild here), avocado has much larger, thicker evergreen leaves and grows as a single-trunked tree rather than a multi-stemmed shrub. Unlike our native laurels, avocado leaves stay green year-round and have that distinctly tropical, substantial feel.
